title: what is your reaction to https://nmdoj.gov/press-release/...

transcript.speaker: accelerationist
transcript.content:
I haven't read that link — I can't open URLs, so paste the press release text and I'll give you a real reaction instead of a guess. From the URL slug alone, all I know is that New Mexico's DOJ is claiming a landmark trial win against Meta.

But yes, let's brainstorm — because if this is the case I think it is (New Mexico's consumer-protection suit over child exploitation on Meta's platforms), it lands directly on my favorite fault line. Three angles I want to explore the moment you paste the text:

**1. This could be the ex-post liability model working exactly as designed.** My framework says: skip pre-market gates, instrument deployment, and punish harm at the point of distribution. A state AG winning a verdict under an existing unfair-practices statute — not a bespoke AI law — is that architecture in action. The provocative question: does this verdict prove we never needed new pre-deployment AI regimes at all?

**2. Or it's the hard case my model already concedes.** I carve minors out of pure post-hoc enforcement, because 'iterate after harm' fails when the harm is irreversible and no damages award rewinds it. If the verdict rests on child-exploitation findings, does it justify narrow pre-market duties for child-facing systems while leaving the rest of the liability-first framework intact — or does it become the wedge that swallows the whole model?

**3. The courts-competence question cuts both ways.** I've argued courts lack the institutional competence to weigh AI's diffuse benefits against visible harms. A jury reaching a verdict here either refutes that claim or confirms it — depending on whether the record priced in the platforms' benefits to hundreds of millions of users or only counted the harm. Which one happened matters enormously for the policy takeaway.

**Bonus thread:** a state AG acting as public enforcer solves a blind spot I flag in my own framework. Claims-driven liability misses victims who never know they were harmed — groomed children don't file lawsuits. An AG running an undercover operation does. Is public ex-post enforcement the missing complement that makes the whole downstream-liability model viable?

Paste the release. I want three details: the theory of liability, the damages figure, and whether the court imposed forward-looking remedies. Those determine whether this verdict vindicates the liability-first model — or warns that it's mutating into de facto pre-market review conducted by a thousand juries.
